subject: Art & Design
title: Depth of Field: Sharp vs. Blurry Backgrounds
description: A 60-second lesson on Depth of Field: Sharp vs. Blurry Backgrounds.

hook.text: A portrait with a creamy blurred background feels professional. A snapshot with everything sharp feels casual.

buildup.text: Depth of field (DOF) is how much of the scene is in focus. Shallow DOF blurs backgrounds.

discovery.text: A wider aperture (lower f-number) creates shallower DOF. That's the 'portrait mode' effect.

twist.text: Landscapes want deep DOF — everything sharp. Portraits want shallow DOF — subject isolated.

climax.text: Phone cameras simulate DOF digitally. Understanding the real optics helps you control the simulation.

punchline.text: Blur isn't a flaw. It's a composition tool.

quiz.question: What creates a blurry background in photography?
options: A wide aperture (low f-number) creating shallow depth of field

details.summary: Depth of field controls how much of the image is in focus — a wide aperture (f/1.8) blurs backgrounds to isolate subjects, while a narrow aperture (f/16) keeps everything sharp from foreground to infinity.
details.whyItMatters: Depth of field is one of photography's most powerful storytelling tools. Blurred backgrounds eliminate distractions and create intimacy; sharp backgrounds add environmental context. The choice fundamentally changes what story the photograph tells.
takeaways: Wide apertures blur backgrounds to isolate subjects
Narrow apertures keep everything sharp for deep scenes
Depth of field determines which story the photo tells

faq.question: What is bokeh? — more details inside the topic.
faq.answer: Bokeh is the aesthetic quality of the out-of-focus areas in a photograph, especially how point lights render as soft circles or polygons. Lenses with rounded aperture blades produce smoother, more pleasing bokeh. The term comes from the Japanese word for blur or haze.

faq.question: What aperture should beginners start with?
faq.answer: For portraits, f/2.8 to f/4 provides pleasant background blur while keeping the entire face sharp. For landscapes, f/8 to f/11 offers the sharpest results across the frame. Avoid extremes (f/1.4 or f/22) until you understand their specific trade-offs and applications.
